subtopic_detail: Restarting a mood stabiliser after eleven days without any doses in a woman whose maintenance dose was previously well tolerated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman with bipolar II disorder maintained on lamotrigine 200 mg daily for three years without any rash or other problem. She went interstate for a funeral, left her tablets at home and has taken none for eleven days.

She feels her mood starting to drop and wants to restart today. She takes no other medication, in particular no sodium valproate and no oral contraceptive. She has had no rash, no fever and no mouth ulceration at any time. She has no intercurrent illness and her renal and liver function were normal three months ago. She asks whether she can simply take her usual 200 mg tonight and carry on as before.

data_table.Examination: Skin entirely clear with no rash anywhere including the mucous membranes, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, mood mildly low with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What should you advise about restarting her medication?

options.text: Restart at her previous maintenance dose tonight because she tolerated it for three years
options.rationale: Resuming the full dose after a gap of this length is the specific prescribing error associated with severe cutaneous reactions, since the risk relates to the rate of dose escalation rather than to cumulative past exposure. Three years of tolerance offers no protection once the drug has washed out. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restart at half her previous maintenance dose and increase to the full dose in one week
options.rationale: Halving the dose still starts far above the recommended initial step and compresses the escalation into a week, which is the pattern the slow schedule exists to prevent. The near pair is that both this and the correct answer re-titrate, but only one uses the original rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Restart at the original starting dose and follow the full titration schedule again
options.rationale: Tolerance to the rash risk is lost after an interruption of about five days or more, so a gap of eleven days means the escalation must begin again from the initial dose with the same slow steps used at first prescription. Previous tolerance of the maintenance dose does not carry over. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to sodium valproate at an equivalent mood stabilising dose to avoid re-titration
options.rationale: Valproate is a recognised mood stabiliser but carries substantial teratogenic risk in a woman of childbearing potential and is subject to pregnancy prevention requirements. Changing agents to avoid a four to six week titration is a disproportionate trade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Restart at her previous maintenance dose with a short course of prophylactic corticosteroid
options.rationale: There is no evidence that corticosteroid cover prevents the cutaneous reaction, and premedicating implies that a fast restart is otherwise acceptable. It also risks masking early rash while the reaction progresses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is effective for maintenance in bipolar disorder, particularly for preventing depressive episodes, and its main hazard is a serious cutaneous reaction that occurs in roughly one in a thousand adults. That risk is driven by how fast the dose is escalated, which is why the initial schedule takes several weeks and why the rate is halved again when the drug is combined with valproate, since valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations. Enzyme inducers including carbamazepine and oestrogen containing contraception have the opposite effect and require higher doses, so starting or stopping the pill changes the level substantially. After any interruption of about five days or more the person is treated as new to the drug and the full titration is repeated, and every patient should be told to stop the drug and seek review immediately if a rash appears.
key_points: The cutaneous risk tracks the rate of escalation, not the cumulative exposure
An interruption of five days or more resets the titration requirement
Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels and halves the starting dose
Oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels
Any rash means stopping the drug and seeking review the same day
explanation.pearls: Starting a combined oral contraceptive can halve the lamotrigine concentration and precipitate relapse, while stopping it can double the level and cause toxicity, so the contraceptive decision and the mood stabiliser dose must be made in the same consultation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after a dose increase of an enzyme inducing mood stabiliser in an older woman with a low serum sodium and concentrated urine
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 74 year old woman brought in by her son because she has been muddled for three days and unsteady on her feet. She has bipolar disorder that has been stable for years, and her psychiatrist increased her carbamazepine from 400 mg to 600 mg daily three weeks ago after a period of irritability.

She takes no diuretic, no antidepressant and no other new medication. She has not vomited or had diarrhoea, she drinks about a litre and a half a day and her son says she has not been thirsty. She has no cough, no weight loss and no headache. She looks euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no oedema, and she is oriented to place but not to the date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Oriented to place and person but not to date, no focal neurological deficit, mild gait unsteadiness, no asterixis, moist mucous membranes with normal skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 252 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), morning cortisol 420 nanomoles per litre, carbamazepine level within the usual target range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the causative drug, restrict fluid and arrange substitution of a different mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Withdrawing the agent and restricting fluid is the correct direction, but stopping an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser abruptly in a woman whose illness has been stable for years risks both seizure and relapse, so the dose is reduced with a planned substitution rather than ceased outright. The near pair is dose reduction against abrupt cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the causative drug dose, restrict fluid intake and recheck her sodium daily
options.rationale: A concentrated urine with urine sodium above 40 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function defines inappropriate antidiuresis, and carbamazepine is among the commonest drug causes with the risk rising after a dose increase and with age. Reducing the dose with fluid restriction corrects it while avoiding abrupt withdrawal, and daily sodium prevents overcorrection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a 500 mL bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and reassess her sodium in six hours
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which shows dry mucous membranes, a postural drop, a raised urea and a urine sodium below 20 mmol/L. Given in this setting it is excreted while the free water is retained, and the sodium can fall further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give 100 mL of 3 per cent hypertonic saline immediately and repeat it twice if needed
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures, coma or other severe neurological manifestations, and she is oriented to place with no focal deficit. Used without that indication it risks correcting the sodium faster than the 8 to 10 mmol/L daily ceiling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral tolvaptan and continue the current dose of her mood stabiliser unchanged
options.rationale: A vasopressin receptor antagonist is a specialist option for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis where the cause cannot be removed, and it requires close monitoring because of rapid correction. Leaving the responsible drug unchanged treats the consequence while the cause continues. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia in a substantial minority of users through a direct antidiuretic effect, and the incidence rises with age, with higher doses and with concurrent diuretics or antidepressants. The biochemical picture is that of inappropriate antidiuresis, with a low serum osmolality, a urine osmolality that is inappropriately high and a urine sodium above 30 to 40 mmol/L in a clinically euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function. Symptoms are non-specific and in older people are commonly attributed to dementia or to the psychiatric illness itself, so a sodium level belongs in the work up of any confusion or fall in someone taking the drug. Management removes or reduces the cause, restricts fluid, and above all corrects slowly, because raising the sodium faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination.
key_points: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are common drug causes of low sodium
Euvolaemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 40 defines the syndrome
Exclude thyroid and adrenal insufficiency before accepting the diagnosis
Hypertonic saline is only for seizures, coma or severe neurological signs
Correction faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L per day risks osmotic demyelination
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium two to four weeks after starting or increasing carbamazepine in anyone over 65, because the fall is usually asymptomatic at first and is the single most common reason the drug has to be abandoned in older patients.

subtopic_detail: Constipation, fatigue and renal colic in a woman on long term lithium with a raised corrected calcium and a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 52 year old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar I disorder for 18 years and has not had an episode in a decade. She passed a kidney stone six weeks ago and has been tired and constipated for several months.

She has no bone pain and no fractures. Her lithium level has been stable between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L on every check, including one taken last week, and she has no tremor, no diarrhoea and no ataxia. She takes no thiazide, no calcium supplement and no vitamin D. Her thyroid function is normal on thyroxine started four years ago. Her mood is euthymic and she is keen to stay on the medication that has kept her well.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no coarse tremor, no ataxia or dysarthria, no proximal weakness, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, no bony tenderness over the spine or long bones
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 8.4 picomoles per litre (1.6-6.9), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nanomoles per litre, creatinine 84 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, lithium 0.7 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her biochemistry?

options.text: Lithium associated overactivity of the parathyroid glands developing over years of use
options.rationale: Lithium raises the set point at which calcium suppresses parathyroid hormone, so the hormone remains inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of a high calcium, and the effect accumulates over years of treatment. The low phosphate and the renal stone fit the same mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Lithium toxicity from accumulation as her renal function has declined over recent years
options.rationale: Toxicity presents with a raised level alongside coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia and confusion, and her level is squarely within range with none of those signs. The near pair is that both are lithium complications, but one is concentration dependent and the other is not. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Malignancy related hypercalcaemia from a solid tumour producing a parathyroid like peptide
options.rationale: Tumour related hypercalcaemia suppresses parathyroid hormone to the bottom of the range because the peptide acts on the same receptor. An unsuppressed hormone excludes that mechanism, and she has no weight loss or other features of malignancy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Excess vitamin D intake causing increased intestinal absorption of dietary calcium
options.rationale: Vitamin D excess raises calcium and phosphate together while suppressing parathyroid hormone, and her phosphate is low with the hormone raised. She also takes no supplement and her vitamin D level is unremarkable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Familial benign hypercalcaemia unmasked by the routine biochemistry taken after the stone
options.rationale: The familial condition gives lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with a characteristically low urinary calcium excretion and rarely causes stones. Her hypercalcaemia is new against previously normal results and it has already produced a stone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Long term lithium requires structured monitoring precisely because its important complications develop slowly and silently. Renal function, thyroid function and calcium are checked every six to twelve months, alongside the lithium level itself, and each one detects a different problem. The calcium abnormality arises because lithium shifts the calcium sensing receptor set point upward, so the parathyroid glands behave as though the calcium is lower than it is, and prevalence rises with duration of treatment to affect a meaningful minority of long term users. Symptoms overlap with both depression and lithium side effects, so fatigue, constipation and low mood in a long term user should prompt a calcium rather than a dose change. Management ranges from observation with monitoring in mild asymptomatic cases through to parathyroid surgery when there is stone disease, bone loss or a substantially elevated calcium, and lithium can often be continued if it remains the only effective treatment.
key_points: Lithium raises the parathyroid set point so the hormone stays unsuppressed
Prevalence increases with duration of treatment over years
Malignant and vitamin D related hypercalcaemia suppress the hormone
Symptoms mimic both depression and lithium side effects
Stone disease or bone loss shifts management towards parathyroid surgery
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics also raise calcium and reduce lithium clearance simultaneously, so adding one to a long term lithium user can produce hypercalcaemia and lithium toxicity in the same fortnight, and the combination needs level and calcium checks within a week of starting.

subtopic_detail: Persistent tongue and jaw movements emerging after years of an antipsychotic in a man already taking benztropine, with no restlessness or subjective urge to move
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for 22 years and benztropine alongside it for most of that time. Over the last eight months his wife has noticed his tongue pushing against his cheek and a chewing movement of his jaw when he is watching television.

He is not distressed by the movements and does not feel any urge to move, and he describes no inner restlessness. The movements stop while he is speaking and are absent in sleep. His psychotic symptoms have been in remission for six years on the current dose. He takes no other medication, has no tremor and no cogwheel rigidity. There are no chorea elsewhere and no family history of a movement disorder.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lateral tongue movements and chewing jaw movements at rest that cease during speech, occasional lip pursing, no truncal or limb chorea, no rigidity or bradykinesia, no tremor, gait normal, Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score 12, no restlessness observed or reported
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Increase the anticholinergic dose and review his involuntary movements in six weeks
options.rationale: Raising the anticholinergic dose is the treatment for drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, and it is the near pair that most often causes harm here because it aggravates these movements measurably. His examination shows no rigidity or bradykinesia to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the antipsychotic dose because the movements reflect inadequate symptom control
options.rationale: A dose increase suppresses the movements briefly by further blocking the same receptors and then worsens the underlying disorder, which is why it is described as masking. His psychosis has been in remission for six years, so there is nothing to treat. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Start propranolol and titrate the dose against the severity of his involuntary movements
options.rationale: Beta blockade is the treatment for the subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move that can accompany antipsychotic treatment, a condition he explicitly does not have. His movements are unaccompanied by any urge and stop during speech. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the anticholinergic and discuss switching to an antipsychotic with lower risk
options.rationale: Anticholinergics worsen this movement disorder rather than helping it, unlike drug induced parkinsonism where they are used, so withdrawing benztropine is the first step and costs nothing. Switching from a high potency first generation agent to one with lower liability, most evidence favouring clozapine, is the next consideration. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic abruptly and monitor his movements over the following three months
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation frequently unmasks or transiently worsens the movements and carries a high risk of psychotic relapse after 22 years of treatment. Any change to the antipsychotic is made gradually and with a plan for maintaining remission. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Involuntary orofacial movements emerging after prolonged dopamine blockade affect a meaningful proportion of long term antipsychotic users, with risk rising with age, duration of exposure, female sex, diabetes and the use of first generation high potency agents. The movements are choreoathetoid, typically begin in the tongue, lips and jaw, are absent in sleep and often suppress during speech or voluntary tongue protrusion, and they are frequently more distressing to family than to the patient. They must be separated from drug induced parkinsonism, which is rigid and bradykinetic and improves with anticholinergics, and from the restlessness syndrome, which carries a subjective urge to move and responds to beta blockade or dose reduction. Management withdraws anticholinergics, reduces or switches the antipsychotic where psychiatric stability allows, and considers a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor where one is available, with regular standardised rating to track change.
key_points: Anticholinergics aggravate these movements and are withdrawn first
Absence of any urge to move separates this from the restlessness syndrome
Increasing the antipsychotic masks the movements and worsens the disorder
Clozapine carries the lowest liability of the available antipsychotics
Standardised rating at each review documents change objectively
explanation.pearls: Standardised rating with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale every six months is recommended for anyone on long term antipsychotic treatment, because the movements are often unnoticed by the patient and a documented baseline is what allows a later change to be attributed correctly.

subtopic_detail: Severe irritability and low mood confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution within days of onset, documented prospectively over two cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33 year old woman who says she becomes a different person for about a week each month, snapping at her children, crying and feeling unable to cope, and that it lifts within two days of her period starting. She feels entirely well for the rest of the month.

You asked her to keep a daily symptom chart and she returns with two complete cycles showing symptoms starting five to seven days before bleeding, peaking on the day before, and absent from day three through to the next luteal phase. She has never had a depressive episode outside this pattern. Her periods are regular at 29 days and not heavy. She is not planning a pregnancy in the next year and uses condoms. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic at the time of consultation on day 9 of her cycle, reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, general and pelvic examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Two cycles of prospective daily symptom ratings confirming luteal onset with resolution by day 3, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 52 micrograms per litre (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only during the luteal phase each cycle
options.rationale: Prospectively confirmed symptoms confined to the luteal phase with complete resolution after menstruation respond to serotonergic treatment within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is why dosing restricted to the second half of the cycle works as well as continuous dosing. It also limits total exposure and side effects. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously with review after eight weeks
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms spill beyond the luteal phase or when cycles are irregular, so the near pair is the schedule rather than the drug. Her charted symptoms are strictly confined to the luteal phase, which makes intermittent dosing the more economical choice. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive taken in an extended regimen with shortened hormone free intervals
options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation helps some women and is a reasonable option for those who also want contraception, but the evidence is weaker than for serotonergic treatment and she is not seeking a hormonal method. It is generally second line for the mood symptoms themselves. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Micronised progesterone taken orally through the second half of each cycle for six cycles
options.rationale: Progesterone supplementation has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for these symptoms and can aggravate them in sensitive women. It persists in practice despite the evidence, which is why it appears here. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back oestrogen and progestogen therapy
options.rationale: Medical suppression of the ovarian cycle is highly effective but is reserved for severe symptoms that have failed serotonergic and hormonal treatment, because of bone loss and menopausal symptoms. It is a specialist step, not a starting point. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Severe premenstrual mood symptoms are distinguished from ordinary premenstrual discomfort by the degree of functional impairment and from an underlying mood or anxiety disorder by the symptom free interval in the follicular phase. Diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings over at least two cycles rather than retrospective recall, because retrospective report agrees poorly with charted symptoms and a substantial proportion of women who describe this pattern turn out to have premenstrual worsening of a continuous disorder instead. That distinction matters because premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive or anxiety disorder is treated by optimising treatment of that disorder rather than by intermittent dosing. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and uniquely act within days in this condition, which allows luteal phase only dosing, and non-pharmacological measures including exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy have supporting evidence.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily ratings are required for the diagnosis
A symptom free follicular phase separates it from a continuous disorder
Serotonergic response occurs within days rather than over weeks
Luteal phase dosing is as effective as continuous dosing here
Progesterone supplementation does not outperform placebo
explanation.pearls: If the charted ratings show symptoms that improve but never fully remit after menstruation, the diagnosis is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying disorder, and intermittent dosing will fail because the baseline condition needs continuous treatment.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Young man requesting a fourth cosmetic procedure for a nose he believes is deformed, with hours of daily mirror checking and an unremarkable appearance to the examiner
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old man who wants a referral to a fourth surgeon about his nose. He has had two rhinoplasties and one revision in three years, each one leaving him briefly relieved and then convinced the result made things worse.

He tells you he spends three or four hours a day checking his profile in reflective surfaces, that he will only leave the house after dark, and that he has stopped seeing friends because he is sure they are looking at it. He has lost his apprenticeship because of absences. He is certain the deformity is real and says he would not need any of this if it were fixed properly. He is not describing voices or other unusual beliefs. His nose appears entirely unremarkable to you.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, no visible nasal deformity or asymmetry on inspection, mood low with reactive affect, no formal thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, belief about the nose held with absolute conviction and not amenable to counter evidence, no other delusional content, passive thoughts that life is not worth living with no current plan
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide the referral, assess his suicide risk and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Adding therapy alongside a fourth procedure still endorses the belief that the nose is the problem and repeats a cycle that has already failed three times. The near pair matters because the therapy is right and the referral is what makes this answer wrong. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start an antipsychotic as monotherapy because his belief is held with complete conviction
options.rationale: Absolute conviction occurs in about a third of people with this disorder and is graded as poor insight rather than reclassified as a psychotic illness, so serotonergic treatment and therapy remain the approach. Antipsychotics are used only as augmentation when response is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Reassure him that his nose looks normal and arrange to review his concerns in one month
options.rationale: Reassurance functions in the same way as his mirror checking, giving momentary relief and reinforcing the preoccupation, and it is one of the behaviours the therapy explicitly targets. It also leaves the suicide risk unassessed for a month. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.text: Refer for assessment of an eating disorder given his preoccupation with his appearance
options.rationale: Appearance preoccupation in an eating disorder centres on weight and body shape and is accompanied by dietary restriction, compensatory behaviours or binge eating. His concern is confined to a single facial feature with no disordered eating described. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders)

options.text: Decline the referral, assess his suicide risk and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Preoccupation with a flaw not observable to others, repetitive checking, avoidance and marked functional loss identifies the disorder, and further surgery predictably fails to relieve it while the risk of suicide in this group is among the highest in psychiatry. Tailored cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is the primary treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder affects around two per cent of the population and is markedly overrepresented in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics, where it is rarely recognised because the presenting request looks ordinary. The diagnosis requires preoccupation with a perceived defect that is not observable or appears slight to others, repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking or reassurance seeking, and clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is frequently absent, and delusional conviction is now treated as a specifier rather than as a separate psychotic disorder, which keeps the treatment pathway the same. Cosmetic procedures almost never help, with most patients reporting the same or worse concern afterwards and many transferring the preoccupation to a new feature. Rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are very high, so risk assessment is part of every consultation.
key_points: The perceived defect is not observable or appears slight to others
Repetitive checking, grooming or reassurance seeking is required
Delusional conviction is a specifier, not a separate psychotic disorder
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and often shift the preoccupation
Suicidal ideation and attempts are substantially more common than average
explanation.pearls: Asking how many hours a day the person spends thinking about the feature separates this from ordinary appearance concern, since an hour or more daily is the working threshold, and most people presenting for repeat cosmetic procedures with this disorder report three hours or more.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder
